Whatever comes first is rain on a tin roof, though I am nowhere near one. I am at a desk in a city where rain comes sideways and windows are sealed with paint. Memory arrives with the wrong soundtrack, insisting on its own weather. I close my eyes and I am seven, under a quilt my grandmother made from scraps of dresses, listening to a storm turn the backyard into a shallow sea. Each drop had a note. I believed if I listened long enough I would learn the song and summon storms whenever I wanted. I never learned it. Maybe that’s why I write—to transcribe music that exists only when no one writes it down.

Then a library at closing time. The lights dim in rows, so shelves go dark like teeth in a smile. A woman in a green coat reads on, oblivious. The librarian, spectacles held together with tape, does not ask her to leave. He waits, pretending to sort returns. He knows a person reading is not just consuming words; she is building a private room inside a public one. To interrupt is to knock down a wall. Small mercies don’t announce themselves as turning points. They happen, and years later you realize you’ve been living in the house they built.

I think about the word threshold. It comes from thresh, separating grain from chaff. A threshold is where you decide what to keep and what to let blow away. Every morning is a threshold. Every conversation. Every sentence. We take the day’s noise and try to find the kernel. Some days there is no kernel, only dust. But dust is also an answer. It tells you the harvest was real.

Then the mind jumps to a subway platform in winter. A saxophonist plays “Summertime,” notes so slow they seem to melt. A man in a construction vest drops a dollar into the case. A child asks her mother why the music is sad. The mother says, “It’s not sad, baby. It’s remembering.” I don’t know if that’s true. I’ve repeated it for years, like a line of poetry that doesn’t belong to me. The train came. We all got on, carrying our separate remembrances like luggage we refused to check.

What else comes? Things I have lost: a blue mitten, a library book, a friend’s number, the exact sound of my father’s laugh. The laugh is hardest. I remember its shape, the way it started in his chest and moved his shoulders, but the sound has been sanded down by time. I try to rebuild it from other laughs, like reconstructing a face from a photograph of a shadow. Grief is not always for people. Sometimes it is for the sensory data of them. The particular timbre. The way they said a word. I have lost “grocery” as my mother said it, stress on the first syllable, long and open, like a door she was happy to walk through. You never know when you are collecting.

A friend told me every city has a hidden river. Even paved over, even routed into pipes, the water remembers. It pulls at foundations. It seeps into basements. The city pretends to be solid, but underneath it negotiates with water. People are like that. We have hidden rivers—old griefs, old joys—running under ordinary days. Sometimes they rise. A song, a smell, a stranger’s accent, and suddenly the pavement is gone and you are standing in the current. You can fight it or let it carry you. The trick is not to drown. The trick is to remember the river is also you.

I wonder what it means to write whatever comes. It means turning on the tap and seeing not water but whatever has settled in the pipes. Rust, a leaf, a memory of rain. It means trusting that strange associations are not random. The brain is a meaning-making machine, and even its accidents are patterned. The saxophonist, the quilt, the librarian with taped glasses are all in the same room, though they never met. That room is a sentence. That room is this one.

Here is the inventory: rain, libraries, thresholds, a subway saxophone, lost mittens, hidden rivers. And now a small lamp, a blank page, the hum of a refrigerator, the sense that someone somewhere is reading this and nodding—not because they know me, but because they have their own rain, their own librarian, their own river. That is the secret of words. They are not bridges between separate islands. They are proof the islands were never separate. Under the water, we have always been connected.

I stop. The rain in my head fades. The page is blank the way a window is blank before you look through it. Whatever comes next is not mine to force. It will come when I am not watching. For now, this is enough. A thousand words, more or less. A room built of them. You are welcome to stay. The door is not locked. It never was.

Then comes the image of a library at closing time. The lights dim in rows, not all at once, so the shelves go dark like teeth in a smile.
